deep.reconstruction:
Context: this note is written in the margin pages of an elementary algebra textbook. It belongs to Gauss's early work on the lemniscatic functions (c. 1797). On this page 'sin', 'cos', s and c mean the lemniscatic sine sl(φ) and cosine cl(φ). They satisfy s² + c² + s²c² = 1, equivalently c² = (1−s²)/(1+s²), and φ = ∫₀^s dx/√(1−x⁴).

(1) Table of special values. 'Theilt man also auch hier die ganze Peripherie in 360°' means the whole lemniscate perimeter 2ϖ is divided into 360°, so 90° ↔ ϖ/2, where sl = 1.
- sl(0) = 0 and sl(90°) = 1.
- sl(45°) = sl(ϖ/4) = √(√2−1) = 0.6435943. This is the bisection value.
- sl(60°) = sl(ϖ/3) = ∜(√12−3) = ∜(2√3−3) = 0.8253788. He rewrites it as ⁸√3 · √(√(3/2) − √(1/2)). Reason (mine): √12−3 = √3(2−√3) and √(2−√3) = √(3/2) − √(1/2). The trailing '⁸√3' is therefore a factor, written after a struck '√3'.
- sl(30°) = sl(ϖ/6) = cl(ϖ/3), using sl(ϖ/2−u) = cl(u). Put a = √(√12−3) = sl²(ϖ/3). Then sl(ϖ/6) = √((1−a)/(1+a)) = (1−a)/√(1−a²) = (1−a)/√(4−√12).

Side rationalisation (right margin) of that last expression:
- Since (√12−3)(4−√12) = 7√12−24, the value equals [√(4−√12) − √(7√12−24)]/(4−√12).
- Multiplying numerator and denominator by 4+√12 (denominator 16−12 = 4) gives (4+√12)[√(4−√12) − √(7√12−24)]/4.
- The struck '(2+√3)(√…' starts the further simplification (4+√12)/4 = (2+√3)/2.
- Completing it (mine): √(4−√12) = √3−1, so sl(ϖ/6) = (1+√3)(1−√(2√3−3))/2 ≈ 0.4354205.
- The unexplained struck '∜(1+√(4/3))' near the top is a cancelled attempt.

(2) Derivatives. A first version is struck: ∂sin = ½(1/c + c)dφ and ∂cos = −½(1/s + s)dφ. These are replaced by:
- ∂sin = 2/(c+1/c) dφ = 2c/(1+c²) dφ = c(1+s²) dφ, using 1+c² = 2/(1+s²).
- ∂cos = −2/(s+1/s) dφ = −2s/(1+s²) dφ = −s(1+c²) dφ.

(3) Maclaurin series (all correct as far as written):
- sl φ = φ − φ⁵/10 + φ⁹/120 − …
- cl φ = 1 − φ² + φ⁴/2 − …
- 1/sl φ = 1/φ + φ³/10 + …
- 1/cl φ = 1 + φ² + φ⁴/2 + …
- Inverse series: φ = ∫ds/√(1−s⁴) = s + (1/2)(1/5)s⁵ + (1·3/2·4)(1/9)s⁹ + (1·3·5/2·4·6)(1/13)s¹³ + …

(4) Lemniscatic tangent. 'By analogy with the circle' he names t = s/c and writes ∂t = [½(1 + 1/c²) + ½(1/c² + s²/c²)] dφ. This is exactly ds/c − s dc/c² evaluated with the struck (wrong) derivative formulas: ds/c = ½(1/c² + 1) and −s dc/c² = ½(1+s²)/c². With the corrected derivatives one gets (mine): dt/dφ = (1+s²) + 2s²/(1−s²) = (1+2s²−s⁴)/(1−s²) = 2/(1+c²) + 2s²/(c²(1+s²)).

The next page goes on to the multiplication formula for sl(4φ) and to higher derivatives of the inverse of dx/X = dy.
errors: The first versions ∂sin = ½(1/c + c)dφ and ∂cos = −½(1/s + s)dφ are wrong; Gauss himself struck them and replaced them with the correct 2/(c+1/c) and −2/(s+1/s).
The final expression for ∂sin is printed as (1+ss)/(cs)·dφ in the transcription. The correct value is c(1+s²)dφ. Either the glyph reads (1+ss)·c, or it is a slip.

The ∂t formula at the bottom is derived from the cancelled, incorrect derivative formulas. At φ = 0 it gives dt/dφ = 3/2 instead of 1. The correct value is (1+2s²−s⁴)/(1−s²). The error was apparently not corrected on this page.
Minor: the series are truncated without an ellipsis; the terms given are correct.

results.modern_name: Special values of the lemniscatic sine (division of the lemniscate into 4, 3, 6 equal parts)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (1796–97, Nachlass/Tagebuch); Fagnano for bisection/trisection-type constructions (1718); later Abel 1827

results.what: Derivatives d sl = cl(1+sl²)dφ = 2/(cl+1/cl)dφ and d cl = −sl(1+cl²)dφ = −2/(sl+1/sl)dφ
results.modern_name: Differential equations of the lemniscatic sine and cosine

results.what: Maclaurin series of sl, cl, 1/sl, 1/cl and inverse series φ = Σ binom(2n,n)/4^n · s^(4n+1)/(4n+1)
results.modern_name: Power series of lemniscatic functions; binomial series of the lemniscatic integral
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, Werke III/X); inverse series essentially Euler/Stirling era

results.what: Definition of the lemniscatic tangent t = sl/cl and attempt at its derivative

deep.surprise_reason: These are early working notes on the lemniscatic functions, a topic well documented as Gauss's from 1797 (Tagebuch, Werke III and X). The special values, derivatives and series are all known parts of his lemniscate theory. Only the details of this draft are new, including a derivative error carried into the tangent formula.

checkable.asserts: the two forms of sl(30°) agree

checkable.sympy: p=symbols('p'); f=p-p**5/10+p**9/120; series(integrate(1/sqrt(1-f**4),(p)) ,p,0,10) if False else series(diff(f,p)**2-(1-f**4),p,0,10)
checkable.asserts: sl series satisfies (sl')² = 1 − sl⁴ to the order given (result O(p**10))
correct derivative of t = s/c is (1+2s²−s⁴)/(1−s²) (0)
Gauss's ∂t formula gives 3/2 at φ=0, showing it is erroneous (correct value 1)

transcription_corrections: In the 60° line, '[-√3-] ⁸√3' should be read as a multiplicative factor: ∜(√12−3) = √(√(3/2)−√(1/2)) · ⁸√3 (a struck '√3' replaced by '⁸√3').
The final form of ∂sin, transcribed as (1+ss)/(cs)·dφ, should mathematically be (1+ss)c·dφ = c(1+s²)dφ; the glyph should be rechecked.
The struck ∂sin line reads ½(1/c + c)dφ (cancelled with vertical strokes), and the struck ∂cos line reads −½(1/s + s)dφ.
